title: Justice and Faith -- Ch. 2: Selected Quotations from Ponencias and Opinions
keywords: the end never justifies the means
primary_topics: Chapter 2 of 'Justice and Faith' -- a curated anthology of direct quotations from CJP's first-two-years ponencias and opinions (1995-1997), arranged in ten lettered topical subsections (A through K, with E omitted)

Subsection A (Substantial Justice) -- Frivaldo + Philippines Today + Leonor + Obosa + Republic v. Sandiganbayan + Guerrero + Tabuena Dissent: law as living instrument against quibblings over patchwork legal technicality; mercy presupposes justice

Subsection B (People's Sovereignty) -- Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority + Santiago v. Comelec Separate Opinion: initiative, referendum and recall as institutionalized legacies of EDSA; majority's burning-the-house-to-exterminate-the-rats critique

Subsection J (Trade and Industry) -- MGG Marine Services + Eriks + Fortune Motors + Manila Prince Hotel Dissent: comptroller's fiduciary duty; foreigners must follow our laws; bidding-as-ridiculous-sham critique against discriminatory judicial legislation

Subsection K (Conduct of Judicial Officers) -- Quiroz v. Orfila + NBI v. Tuliao + Valat v. Judge Ramos: government employees bound by rules of proper and ethical behavior; sheriffs play important role; ignorance of law on the part of a judge is most ignominious
sub_topics: Substantial-justice signature -- 'The real essence of justice does not emanate from quibblings over patchwork legal technicality. It proceeds from the spirit's gut consciousness of the dynamic role of law as a brick in the ultimate development of the social edifice' (Frivaldo v. Comelec, 1996)

Each-case-has-flesh-and-blood maxim -- 'General principles do not decide specific cases...Each case has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles' (Philippines Today v. NLRC, 1997)
Not-a-toothless-promoter-of-niceties -- 'The Supreme Court... cannot shrink from its quintessential role as the fountain of speedy, adequate and substantial justice' (Leonor v. CA, 1996)

Letter-killeth-spirit-giveth-life -- 'Law should not be read and interpreted in isolated academic abstraction nor even for the sake of logical symmetry but always in [the] context of pulsating social realities and specific environmental facts' (Obosa v. CA, 1997)

PCG/Sandiganbayan policy -- 'set aside technicalities and formalities that serve merely to delay or impede their judicious resolution... Eleven years have passed since the government started its search... The definitive resolution of such cases on the merits is thus long overdue' (Republic v. Sandiganbayan, 1997)
Speedy-disposition limits -- 'a party's individual rights should not work against and preclude the people's equally important right to public justice' (Guerrero v. CA, 1996)

Tabuena Dissent -- Nuremberg analogy: '[T]he defendants were military officers of the Third Reich...dutybound to obey direct orders on pain of court martial and death at a time when their country was at war...Nonetheless, they were meted out death sentences by hanging or long-term imprisonments'; '[a] moral choice was not only possible. It was in fact available to the accused. They could have opted to defy the illegal order, with no risk of court martial or death. Or they could have resigned'

Justice-before-mercy hierarchy -- 'Mercy and compassion are virtues which are cherished in every civilized society. But before they can be invoked, there must first be justice...the legal and natural precedence and order of things: justice first before mercy' (Tabuena Dissent, 1997)

Initiative-as-EDSA-legacy -- 'Initiative, like referendum and recall, is a new and treasured feature of the Filipino constitutional system. All three are institutionalized legacies of the world-admired EDSA people power' (Santiago v. Comelec Separate Opinion, 1997)

Burning-the-house-to-exterminate-the-rats critique of majority position in Santiago -- '[I]t is equivalent to burning the whole house to exterminate the rats, and to killing the patient to relieve him of pain'

Subsection J -- MGG Marine Services v. NLRC and Molina (1996): comptroller-finance-officer's duty of controlling cash flow and following specific instructions -- extremely-oppressive-and-cruel to require petitioners to retain such admittedly untrustworthy officer in 'the innermost sanctum of management'
Eriks v. CA (1997) -- develop trade relations but enforce laws regulating foreigners; foreigners must subject themselves to reasonable regulation
Fortune Motors (1997) -- wholesale automotive financing scheme explained at length as exemplar of CJP's pedagogical opening style

Manila Prince Hotel Dissent (1997) -- bidding-as-ridiculous-sham critique against judicial legislation that lets Filipino losers match foreigner winners; 'unfairness, greed and isolation are self-defeating and in the long-term, self-destructing'; do-not-do-unto-others-what-you-do-not-want-others-to-do-unto-you closing

Subsection K -- government employees 'bound by the rules of proper and ethical behavior... expected to act with self-restraint and civility at all times, even when confronted with rudeness and insolence' (Quiroz v. Orfila); sheriffs as agents-of-the-law with high standards (NBI v. Tuliao); ignorance-of-the-law-on-the-part-of-a-judge as most ignominious (Valat v. Ramos)

stances.claim: The real essence of justice does not emanate from quibblings over patchwork legal technicality -- it proceeds from the spirit's gut consciousness of the dynamic role of law as a brick in the ultimate development of the social edifice; the Court struggled against the easy, legalistic, technical and sometimes harsh anachronisms of the law in order to evoke substantial justice (Frivaldo v. Comelec, 1996).
stances.rhetorical_move: gut-consciousness-of-dynamic-role-of-law titular framing + brick-in-social-edifice metaphor + harsh-anachronisms-resisted-for-substantial-justice signature thesis

stances.claim: Each case has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles -- the circumstances of time, place, event, person, and particularly attendant circumstances and actions before, during and after the operative fact should all be taken in their totality so that justice can be rationally and fairly dispensed (Philippines Today v. NLRC, 1997).
stances.rhetorical_move: flesh-and-blood metaphor + clinical-classroom-principles negation + totality-of-circumstances ethic

stances.claim: The Supreme Court is not just a toothless promoter of procedural niceties which are understood and appreciated only by lawyers and jurists -- it cannot shrink from its quintessential role as the fountain of speedy, adequate and substantial justice (Leonor v. CA, 1996).
stances.rhetorical_move: not-a-toothless-promoter-of-niceties rebuke + fountain-of-justice titular metaphor + neither-purse-nor-sword qualifier

stances.claim: Law must be understood not by 'the letter that killeth but by the spirit that giveth life' -- it should not be read and interpreted in isolated academic abstraction nor even for the sake of logical symmetry, but always in the context of pulsating social realities and specific environmental facts (Obosa v. CA, 1997).

Mercy and compassion are virtues which are cherished in every civilized society, but before they can be invoked, there must first be justice -- the Supreme Court's duty is to render justice, while the power to dispense pardon lies elsewhere; the Constitution ordains a final conviction by the courts before the President can exercise his power to wipe away the penalty (Tabuena Dissent, 1997).
stances.rhetorical_move: mercy-and-compassion-presupposing-justice hierarchy + court-renders-justice-pardon-power-lies-elsewhere institutional disambiguation + justice-first-before-mercy closing

stances.claim: A moral choice was not only possible -- it was in fact available to the accused; they could have opted to defy the illegal order, with no risk of court martial or death; or they could have resigned (Tabuena Dissent, 1997).
stances.rhetorical_move: Nuremberg analogy + moral-choice-was-not-only-possible-but-available rebuttal + defy-or-resign alternative test
stances.confidence: CJP-asserted as Tabuena Dissent moral-agency standard

stances.claim: Initiative, like referendum and recall, is a new and treasured feature of the Filipino constitutional system -- all three are institutionalized legacies of the world-admired EDSA people power; their misuse and abuse must be resolutely struck down, but their legitimate exercise should be carefully nurtured and zealously protected (Santiago v. Comelec Separate Opinion, 1997).
stances.rhetorical_move: EDSA-legacy framing + treasured-feature + dual posture (struck-down-when-misused / nurtured-when-legitimate)

stances.claim: Ignorance of the law on the part of a judge is not only most ignominious, it is also prejudicial to litigants and the administration of justice as a whole -- magistrates are well-advised to keep abreast of the latest in legislation and jurisprudence, and avoid dealing out injustice and reaping embarrassment for themselves (Valat v. Judge Ramos, 1996).
stances.rhetorical_move: most-ignominious adjective intensifier + prejudicial-to-administration-of-justice institutional stake + dealing-out-injustice-and-reaping-embarrassment closing rebuke

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 2 of 'Justice and Faith' is a curated anthology of direct quotations from CJP's first-two-years ponencias and opinions (October 1995 to October 1997), arranged in ten lettered topical subsections (A through K, with E omitted): A. On Promoting Substantial Justice, B. On Upholding the People's Sovereignty, C. On Protecting the People's Rights, D. On Interpreting the Constitution and the Laws, F. On Protecting Human Life, G. On Comforting the Innocent, H. On Compassion for the Repentant, I. On Promoting Cultural Values and Religious Faith, J. On Enhancing Trade and Industry, and K. On the Conduct of Judicial Officers. Signature passages anchor each section -- from Frivaldo v. Comelec's titular 'the real essence of justice does not emanate from quibblings over patchwork legal technicality. It proceeds from the spirit's gut consciousness of the dynamic role of law as a brick in the ultimate development of the social edifice'; through Philippines Today v. NLRC's 'each case has its own flesh and blood and cannot be decided simply on the basis of isolated clinical classroom principles'; Leonor v. CA's 'the Supreme Court is not just a toothless promoter of procedural niceties... [but] the fountain of speedy, adequate and substantial justice'; Obosa v. CA's 'law must be understood not by the letter that killeth but by the spirit that giveth life'; the Tabuena Dissent's Nuremberg-analogy holding that 'a moral choice was not only possible. It was in fact available' and that 'before [mercy] can be invoked, there must first be justice'; Santiago v. Comelec's Separate Opinion treating initiative, referendum and recall as 'institutionalized legacies of the world-admired EDSA people power' that must be 'carefully nurtured and zealously protected' while abuse is 'resolutely struck down'; the Manila Prince Hotel Dissent's bidding-as-ridiculous-sham critique with its closing 'do not do unto others what you do not want others to do unto you'; and Valat v. Judge Ramos's standard that 'ignorance of the law on the part of a judge is not only most ignominious, it is also prejudicial to litigants and the administration of justice as a whole.' Together the subsections present CJP's signature doctrinal voice across his first two years on the bench.
